script.opening: (Defensive, a bit ashamed, sitting in his taxi between fares.) "So you're saying I need to go on insulin now. Honestly, that feels like I've failed — like I haven't tried hard enough. And insulin… my mum went on insulin, then she went blind, then everything fell apart. I don't want to end up like that. And I drive a taxi all day — I can't be having funny turns at the wheel. I really don't want needles."

facts.text: "Because the tablets were meant to work. If I need injections, it means I messed up."

"I take them. Mostly. The odd one goes if I'm on a long shift." Metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide 160 mg twice daily, sitagliptin 100 mg daily. Tried semaglutide injections last year — stopped after 2 months due to nausea.
"No, never had that" — no shakes, sweats or confusion so far. Doesn't test his sugar at home; has no meter.

"Nothing I've really noticed" — if asked specifically: thirsty, up twice a night to pass urine, tired. No weight loss. No eye or foot problems so far; retinal screening last year showed "a few spots" (background retinopathy).
"Council licence, yes. Long days, ten hours sometimes." Private hire driver, 6 days a week. Has never had to tell the DVLA anything.

"Her sugar was bad for years. Then they put her on insulin, and after that her eyes went, then her kidneys. She died. So in my head, insulin is where it all goes wrong." She was diagnosed in her forties and rarely saw a doctor.

Type 2 diabetes for 12 years. High blood pressure (ramipril) and cholesterol (atorvastatin). No allergies. Non-smoker, doesn't drink. Married, three children (youngest 16). BMI 29. Eats one big meal late at night after shifts.
"Honestly, that you'd say I can try harder with the tablets instead."

Defensive and frightened. If the doctor pushes insulin without exploring his beliefs, become firmer: "I'm not doing it." Softens when told it isn't his fault: "So it's not because I've been rubbish." Main worry: "And the driving? That's my living." Accepts honest DVLA advice: "I'd rather know now than get caught out." Prefers learning with a nurse: "If I can see it, I think I can do it."

ice.ideas: "Insulin means I've failed — and it's what made my mum go blind."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear of ending up like his mother; fear of needles; fear of a hypo at the wheel and of losing his taxi licence and income.
ice.expectations: "To stay on tablets and try harder."

cues: "My mum went blind." — explore what he thinks caused it.
"I drive a taxi all day." — livelihood and DVLA.

checkpoints.text: ELICITS and reframes the "insulin = failure" belief — explaining type 2 diabetes is progressive (declining pancreatic insulin) so insulin reflects the natural course, not lack of effort — validating the feeling while correcting it
Explores and corrects the "insulin caused my mum’s blindness" misattribution — complications reflect poorly controlled diabetes/era, and good control (which insulin aids) REDUCES complication risk

Provides practical education — reassurance re fine near-painless needles, injection technique/site rotation, the NICE NG28 regimen (basal, or basal plus short/rapid-acting from the start with HbA1c ≥75), titration and sulfonylurea review — and arranges DSN/structured-education support

Counsels HYPOGLYCAEMIA thoroughly: recognition, treatment with 15–20 g fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck at 10–15 minutes, then longer-acting snack, carrying carbs, risk factors (missed meals, alcohol, exercise) and when to seek help

Covers the DVLA/DRIVING duty for insulin — must inform DVLA (insulin >3 months), check glucose within 2 hours before and every 2 hours while driving (≤5.0 eat first; <4.0 do not drive, wait 45 minutes after recovery), carry fast-acting carbs, tell his taxi licensing authority, which applies the stricter Group 2 standard — and documents the advice
Surfaces the layered FEAR (failure, his mother’s fate, hypos, losing his licence) empathically and corrects misconceptions WITH the patient rather than overriding him with facts
Frames the driving issue supportively (good management usually permits continued driving), checks understanding, and works toward a SHARED decision rather than coercion or capitulation

Safety-nets and follows up: DSN referral/structured education, hypo and sick-day rules, the DVLA notification and driving advice documented, titration and review plan, and complication-screening reassurance — a shared, well-supported insulin start, not facts-over-fear or accepting poor control

worked.txt: "I really hear that this feels like failure — but I want to gently challenge that. Type 2 diabetes changes over the years; the body makes less of its own insulin, so needing it now is just the natural course, not you not trying hard enough. Lots of people reach this point."

worked.lbl: Address the fear about his mum
worked.txt: "Tell me about your mum … I’m so sorry. Here’s something important, though: it wasn’t the insulin that caused her blindness — that comes from diabetes being out of control for a long time. Good control, which insulin helps with, actually PROTECTS your eyes, kidneys and nerves. We’re using it to avoid her path, not repeat it."

"The needles aren’t what you’re picturing — they’re tiny and most people say they barely feel them. We might start with one injection a day, though with your sugar level we should also talk about adding a quick-acting one at meals from the start, and our diabetes nurse will show you exactly how and support you. We’d also look again at your gliclazide, because with insulin it adds to the hypo risk. Would it help to see one now?"

"The thing to know about is a ‘hypo’ — blood sugar dropping too low: sweaty, shaky, hungry. The fix is simple — something sugary like glucose tabs or juice, check again after 10 to 15 minutes, then a snack. You’ll always carry fast sugar. Knowing this makes it very manageable."

"Because you drive for a living, two musts: you have to tell the DVLA you’re on insulin, and your council licensing team, who use the stricter lorry and bus standard for taxis. You check your sugar within 2 hours before driving and every 2 hours on shift — ‘five to drive’: at 5 or below, eat something first. Below 4, or feeling hypo, don’t drive, and wait 45 minutes after it’s back to normal. With good control, people carry on driving fine — this protects your licence, it doesn’t automatically end it."

"I don’t want to push insulin on you — I want you to feel okay about it. How does it sound now we’ve talked it through? Let’s get the diabetes nurse involved, start gently, and review closely. You’re not doing this alone."

f.learning: Starting insulin in type 2 diabetes is as much about BELIEFS and SAFETY as pharmacology. Elicit and reframe the common feeling that insulin means personal FAILURE: type 2 diabetes is PROGRESSIVE — the pancreas makes less insulin over time — so needing insulin reflects the natural course, not a lack of effort, and is a positive, effective step. Explore and correct the frequent misattribution that "insulin caused my relative’s blindness/decline": complications such as retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy arise from poorly controlled diabetes (and, for older relatives, an earlier treatment era), whereas good glucose control — which insulin helps achieve — REDUCES that risk. Provide practical education (fine, near-painless pen needles; technique and site rotation; a basal-insulin start titrated to fasting glucose, or — per NICE NG28 — basal plus short- or rapid-acting insulin from the start when HbA1c is 75 mmol/mol or higher; review of a sulfonylurea; DSN/structured-education support). Counsel HYPOGLYCAEMIA thoroughly — recognition (sweating, tremor, hunger, palpitations, confusion), treatment with 15–20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, rechecked after 10–15 minutes, then a longer-acting snack (JBDS-IP), always carrying carbs, risk factors (missed meals, alcohol, exercise) and when to seek help. Critically, cover the DVLA/DRIVING duty for insulin: the patient MUST inform the DVLA if insulin will last more than 3 months, check glucose no more than 2 hours before driving and every 2 hours while driving (5.0 mmol/L or below — eat before driving; below 4.0 — do not drive, and wait 45 minutes after recovery), carry fast-acting carbohydrate, and never drive with impaired hypo awareness (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive, November 2025 edition; INF294) — and a taxi driver, though licensed under Group 1, must also tell the council licensing authority, which generally applies the stricter Group 2 standard (no severe hypo in 12 months, twice-daily monitoring, CGM allowed since November 2025); advise clearly, document, and frame supportively because good management usually permits continued driving. The hidden agenda is layered fear (failure, a relative’s fate, hypos, losing licence/income); surface and address each empathically, equip the patient with hypo and driving knowledge, involve the DSN, and reach a SHARED decision — neither overriding fear with facts alone nor capitulating to ongoing poor control.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG28 (type 2 diabetes in adults: management, updated February 2026) · [2] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: a guide for medical professionals (November 2025 edition) · [3] DVLA INF294, A guide to insulin-treated diabetes and driving · [4] JBDS-IP, Hospital management of hypoglycaemia in adults with diabetes · [5] BNF insulin monographs
knowledge.summary: Needing insulin reflects progressive loss of beta-cell function, not failure. Starting it safely means a structured programme: technique, self-monitoring, titration, hypoglycaemia and the DVLA rules. For a taxi driver the licensing conversation is part of the prescription, not an afterthought.

points.t: NICE NG28 [1] (insulin recommendations amended 2026 for product withdrawals and shortages): offer NPH insulin once or twice daily according to need, or a basal insulin intended for once- or twice-daily use, as initial insulin therapy. Consider basal plus short- or rapid-acting insulin from the start, especially if HbA1c is 75 mmol/mol or higher — his is 86. Continue metformin unless contraindicated and review the other agents, particularly a sulfonylurea (hypoglycaemia risk). Doses per BNF [5].

NICE NG28 [1]: anyone starting insulin gets a structured programme covering injection technique (rotating sites, avoiding repeated injections at one point), self-monitoring, dose titration to target, dietary advice, the DVLA guidance [2], managing hypoglycaemia, managing acute changes in glucose, and support from a professional trained in insulin therapy.

Type 2 diabetes is progressive: beta-cell insulin output falls over time, so most people eventually need treatment intensification. Validate the feeling, then correct the belief. Needing insulin says nothing about his effort.

Retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy follow years of hyperglycaemia. Insulin did not blind his mother; better control lowers his risk. Check his retinal screening is up to date before glucose is brought down.

Symptoms: sweating, tremor, hunger, palpitations, confusion. Treat with 15–20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck after 10–15 minutes and repeat if still low, then a longer-acting carbohydrate (JBDS-IP [4]). Risks: missed meals, alcohol, unplanned exercise, dose errors, a sulfonylurea alongside.

DVLA [2][3]: notify if insulin treatment will last more than 3 months. Check glucose no more than 2 hours before driving and every 2 hours while driving (CGM is permitted, with finger-prick backup). 5.0 mmol/L or below — eat a snack before driving. Below 4.0 mmol/L or hypo symptoms — do not drive; treat, and wait 45 minutes after glucose is back to normal. Must not drive with impaired awareness, or after two or more severe (assisted) hypos while awake in 12 months.

Council taxi and private hire licensing authorities generally apply the DVLA Group 2 medical standard. Group 2 on insulin [2]: full hypo awareness, no severe hypo in the previous 12 months, glucose monitored at least twice daily including non-driving days (CGM allowed for Group 2 since November 2025, with finger-prick backup), and a specialist assessment. He should contact his licensing authority before he starts, so any gap in work is planned rather than a shock.

Record the hypoglycaemia and DVLA advice, that he was told to notify the DVLA and his licensing authority, and his decision. The duty to notify is his; the GMC expects the doctor to explain it and act if a patient keeps driving against advice.

model.text: Hello Mr Mehta, it’s Dr Khan. Thank you for joining on video. I know the last review mentioned insulin — before I say anything, how are you feeling about that?
model.why: Opens with his feelings, not the HbA1c

model.text: Honestly, it feels like I’ve failed. Like I didn’t try hard enough. My mum went on insulin, then she went blind, then everything fell apart. And I drive a taxi all day — I can’t be having funny turns. I don’t want needles.

That’s a lot to be carrying, and thank you for being so straight with me. I can hear four worries: feeling you’ve failed, what happened to your mum, the needles, and your driving. I’d like to take each one seriously. Can we go through them, and then decide together what to do?
model.why: Summarises the layered concerns and sets a shared agenda

model.text: Yeah. Okay.
Let’s start with the failure part. What makes it feel that way to you?
model.why: Explores the belief before correcting it

model.text: Because the tablets were meant to work. If I need injections, it means I messed up.
Can I ask how you get on with the tablets day to day — do any get missed, or cause you problems?
model.why: Checks adherence and tolerability before escalating

model.text: I take them. Mostly. The odd one goes if I’m on a long shift.
Thanks, that’s honest. Have you had any times when you felt shaky, sweaty or muddled, as if your sugar had dropped?
model.why: Screens current hypoglycaemia, relevant to the regimen and his licence

model.text: No, never had that.
And have you noticed more thirst, passing more urine, or losing weight without trying?
Nothing I’ve really noticed.
Tell me about the driving. Is it a council taxi licence, and how long are your shifts?
model.why: Establishes his licence type — taxi work usually follows the stricter Group 2 medical standard

model.text: Council licence, yes. Long days, ten hours sometimes.
You mentioned your mum. Would you tell me what happened to her?
Her sugar was bad for years. Then they put her on insulin, and after that her eyes went, then her kidneys. She died. So in my head, insulin is where it all goes wrong.

I’m really sorry. Watching that would make anyone wary. Can I share something that might change how that looks? Blindness in diabetes comes from sugar being high for a long time, which damages the small vessels at the back of the eye. By the time your mum started insulin, that damage had probably already been done. The insulin didn’t cause it — the years of high sugar did.
model.why: Corrects the misattribution of complications to insulin

model.text: I never thought of it like that.
And that’s why I’m suggesting it now, while your eyes and kidneys are protected. We’re using insulin to avoid her path, not to repeat it. What were you hoping would happen today?
model.why: Links the correction to his fear and elicits expectations

model.text: Honestly, that you’d say I can try harder with the tablets instead.

Here’s the honest picture. Your long-term sugar test is 86 — well above where we’d want it. Type 2 diabetes changes over the years; the pancreas makes less insulin, so the same tablets do less. Needing insulin is the natural course, not you failing. Plenty of people who work hard at it reach this point.
model.why: Explains progression in plain language and reframes failure

model.text: So it’s not because I’ve been rubbish.

No. And the needles are nothing like a blood-test needle — they’re very fine pen needles, and most people barely feel them. We’d usually start with a background insulin, and because your level is quite high we may add a mealtime dose too. Our diabetes nurse will show you exactly how, and you’d keep your metformin. We’d look at your other tablets as well — some can cause lows once insulin starts.
model.why: NG28-consistent regimen, practical reassurance and review of hypoglycaemic agents

model.text: And the driving? That’s my living.

This matters, so I’ll be clear. On insulin, you must tell the DVLA, and because taxi licensing usually uses the stricter rules for professional drivers, you should also speak to the council before you start. They’ll want you to have good awareness of lows, no severe lows, and regular glucose readings. I can’t promise there won’t be any pause in work while they check, but people do carry on driving taxis on insulin — and knowing the rules is what protects your licence.
model.why: Gives accurate DVLA and licensing-authority advice honestly

model.text: Right. I’d rather know now than get caught out.

Then the daily rule: check your sugar within two hours before you drive and every two hours on shift. If it’s 5 or under, eat something before you set off. Under 4, or you feel a low coming, don’t drive — treat it and wait 45 minutes after it’s back to normal. Keep glucose tablets in the cab.
model.why: Specific DVLA glucose rules for a working driver

model.text: And for a low anywhere: sweaty, shaky, hungry, muddled. Take fast sugar — glucose tablets or a small sugary drink — check again after 10 to 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then a sandwich or biscuits. Missed meals and alcohol are the big triggers. How does that sound?
More manageable than I thought.

So where are you now? You don’t have to decide this minute. We could book you with the diabetes nurse for an injection demonstration, you contact the council, and we decide together once you’ve seen it.
model.why: Shared decision without coercion or capitulation

model.text: Let’s do the nurse. If I can see it, I think I can do it.

Good. I’ll also make sure your eye screening is up to date, and I’ll note today that I’ve told you about the DVLA and the council. Could you tell me back the two driving rules, so I know I’ve explained them properly?
model.why: Documents the advice and checks understanding with teach-back

model.text: Test before I drive and every two hours. Under 5, eat first. Under 4, don’t drive, sort it, wait 45 minutes. And tell the DVLA and the council.

Spot on. Once you start, if you have a low that needs someone else’s help, stop driving and tell us. If you’re ill and not eating, ring us for sick-day advice rather than stopping insulin. I’ll see you after the nurse appointment. Anything we’ve not covered?
model.why: Clear safety-net, sick-day advice and follow-up

model.text: No — I feel a lot better. Thanks, doc.
You’ve not failed at anything. You’re taking the step that protects your eyes, your health and your job.

social.t: Taxi driving is his livelihood; any licensing pause means lost income. Plan the timing of insulin with him and his licensing authority.
His mother’s blindness and death shape his beliefs about insulin. Explore it; don’t dismiss it.

legal.t: Insulin-treated drivers must notify the DVLA if treatment will last more than 3 months; glucose within 2 hours before driving and 2-hourly while driving (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive, November 2025; INF294).

Council taxi and private hire licensing usually applies the Group 2 medical standard: full awareness, no severe hypo in 12 months, regular monitoring and specialist assessment. He must inform his licensing authority.

GMC Confidentiality (2017) and its guidance on reporting concerns to the DVLA: the patient has the legal duty to notify. If he keeps driving when unsafe and won’t stop, the doctor may inform the DVLA after telling him.

professional.t: GMC Decision making and consent (2020): present options, benefits and risks, including what happens if he declines insulin; respect his choice and keep the door open.
Record hypo teaching, DVLA and licensing advice, and his decision.

community.t: Diabetes specialist nurse, structured education programme for insulin, and Diabetes UK information on insulin and driving.

redFlags: Symptomatic hyperglycaemia: thirst, polyuria, weight loss — consider urgency and ketones if unwell
Any current hypoglycaemia, especially while driving
Impaired hypo awareness or a severe (assisted) hypo — driving implications
psychosocial: Taxi work: licence type, shift length, income dependence
His mother’s illness and death and what it taught him about insulin
Practical barriers: injecting on shift, storage, eating patterns
ice: Idea: insulin means he failed, and insulin caused his mother’s blindness
Concern: hypos at the wheel and losing his licence and income
Expectation: to be allowed to try harder with tablets

playbook.diagnosis: Type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 86 mmol/mol despite maximal oral therapy — insulin is indicated per NICE NG28, with a structured programme and DVLA counselling.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your pancreas makes less insulin as the years go on — like a battery that runs down. The tablets can only push it so far. Insulin tops up what your body can’t make any more. That’s the illness moving on, not you failing.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought insulin caused your mum’s blindness. It was the years of high sugar. Starting now is how you avoid her path.”
management.psychosocial: Plan around his shifts: timing with the council, glucose checks in the cab, carbohydrate in the car, a DSN session he can fit around work.
sharedPlan: DSN demonstration and structured insulin programme (NICE NG28)
NG28 regimen: NPH or basal once or twice daily; consider adding short- or rapid-acting insulin with HbA1c ≥75; keep metformin; review sulfonylurea
Notify DVLA; contact licensing authority before starting; retinal screening up to date
safetyNet: Hypo: 15–20 g fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 10–15 minutes, then a longer-acting snack; a severe hypo means stop driving and tell us
Sick-day advice: don’t stop insulin when unwell; ring for advice

pitfalls.intro: Candidates rarely fail this station on insulin pharmacology. They fail on beliefs left unaddressed, vague or wrong driving advice, and a decision that is either forced or abandoned.

items.fail: “Insulin isn’t a failure” said in the first minute, before hearing why he feels that way.
items.why: Reassurance before exploration reads as dismissal; the examiner marks a missed cue.
items.fix: Ask what makes it feel like failure, then reframe with the progressive nature of the disease.

items.fail: Moving past “my mum went blind” with a brief “sorry to hear that”.
items.why: The misattribution is the main obstacle. Leaving it intact means he leaves still believing insulin blinds people.
items.fix: Ask what happened, then explain that long-term high glucose caused her complications and insulin protects him.

items.fail: “Just tell the DVLA” with no rules, or wrong thresholds.
items.why: Driving advice is central for a taxi driver. Incomplete advice is a patient-safety fail.
items.fix: Give the rules: check within 2 hours before and every 2 hours; 5.0 or below eat; under 4.0 don’t drive, treat, wait 45 minutes. Carry glucose.

items.fail: Treating a council taxi licence like an ordinary car licence.
items.why: Licensing authorities usually apply the Group 2 standard; missing it can cost him his job unexpectedly.
items.fix: Ask what licence he holds and tell him to contact the licensing authority before starting.

items.fail: Starting insulin without hypoglycaemia teaching or a review of the sulfonylurea.
items.why: NICE NG28 requires hypo management in the structured programme; a sulfonylurea plus insulin raises the risk.
items.fix: Teach recognition and treatment, and say you will review the tablets that cause lows.

items.fail: Pressing for a yes today, or accepting “no” and ending with nothing.
items.why: Both fail shared decision-making. The station rewards a supported next step.
items.fix: Offer the DSN demonstration, a decision date and documented advice. Check understanding with teach-back.

timeMap.d: He arrives with four worries in one breath. Let him finish, then name them back to him.
Adherence, current hypos, hyperglycaemic symptoms, licence type (council taxi) and shift pattern.
Ask what happened to her. Correct the belief that insulin caused her blindness.
Progressive disease, fine needles, NG28 regimen, DVLA and council rules, hypo treatment.
Shared decision (DSN demonstration), document driving advice, teach-back, sick-day and severe-hypo safety-net.

wordPics.fail: Tells him he needs insulin and brushes off the failure and blindness beliefs; no hypoglycaemia teaching; no DVLA advice or a wrong rule; ignores that taxi licensing is stricter; pushes insulin or gives in with no plan.
wordPics.pass: Reframes insulin as the natural course of type 2 diabetes; corrects the blindness misattribution; explains hypo recognition and treatment; tells him he must notify the DVLA and gives the glucose-before-driving rule; refers to the DSN.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: asks about his mother and uses her story to show why control protects him; identifies the council licence and the stricter standard; is honest that there may be a pause; reviews the sulfonylurea risk; teach-back of the driving rules; a genuinely shared decision that he owns.

avoid.dont: “Lots of people are on insulin, it’s nothing to worry about.”
avoid.instead: “You watched what diabetes did to your mum. Can we talk about what really caused her sight loss?”
avoid.why: Blanket reassurance skips the belief that is driving his refusal.

avoid.dont: “You’ll be fine to drive, just be careful.”
avoid.instead: “On insulin you must tell the DVLA, and speak to the council before you start — here are the exact rules.”
avoid.why: Vague driving advice is unsafe and fails the Tasks domain.

avoid.dont: “If you won’t have insulin, there’s nothing else I can do.”
avoid.instead: “You don’t have to decide today. Let’s see the nurse, look at it together, and decide.”
avoid.why: Ultimatums end the relationship; shared decisions keep him engaged.

That’s a lot to be carrying, and thank you for being so straight with me. I can hear four worries: feeling you’ve failed, what happened to your mum, the needles, and your driving. I’d like to take each one seriously. Can we go through them, and then decide together what to do?
SCA_MODELS.why: Summarises the layered concerns and sets a shared agenda

SCA_MODELS.text: Yeah. Okay.
Let’s start with the failure part. What makes it feel that way to you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explores the belief before correcting it

SCA_MODELS.text: Because the tablets were meant to work. If I need injections, it means I messed up.
Can I ask how you get on with the tablets day to day — do any get missed, or cause you problems?
SCA_MODELS.why: Checks adherence and tolerability before escalating

SCA_MODELS.text: I take them. Mostly. The odd one goes if I’m on a long shift.
Thanks, that’s honest. Have you had any times when you felt shaky, sweaty or muddled, as if your sugar had dropped?
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens current hypoglycaemia, relevant to the regimen and his licence

SCA_MODELS.text: No, never had that.
And have you noticed more thirst, passing more urine, or losing weight without trying?
Nothing I’ve really noticed.
Tell me about the driving. Is it a council taxi licence, and how long are your shifts?
SCA_MODELS.why: Establishes his licence type — taxi work usually follows the stricter Group 2 medical standard

SCA_MODELS.text: Council licence, yes. Long days, ten hours sometimes.
You mentioned your mum. Would you tell me what happened to her?
Her sugar was bad for years. Then they put her on insulin, and after that her eyes went, then her kidneys. She died. So in my head, insulin is where it all goes wrong.

I’m really sorry. Watching that would make anyone wary. Can I share something that might change how that looks? Blindness in diabetes comes from sugar being high for a long time, which damages the small vessels at the back of the eye. By the time your mum started insulin, that damage had probably already been done. The insulin didn’t cause it — the years of high sugar did.
SCA_MODELS.why: Corrects the misattribution of complications to insulin

SCA_MODELS.text: I never thought of it like that.
And that’s why I’m suggesting it now, while your eyes and kidneys are protected. We’re using insulin to avoid her path, not to repeat it. What were you hoping would happen today?
SCA_MODELS.why: Links the correction to his fear and elicits expectations

SCA_MODELS.text: Honestly, that you’d say I can try harder with the tablets instead.

Here’s the honest picture. Your long-term sugar test is 86 — well above where we’d want it. Type 2 diabetes changes over the years; the pancreas makes less insulin, so the same tablets do less. Needing insulin is the natural course, not you failing. Plenty of people who work hard at it reach this point.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains progression in plain language and reframes failure

SCA_MODELS.text: So it’s not because I’ve been rubbish.

No. And the needles are nothing like a blood-test needle — they’re very fine pen needles, and most people barely feel them. We’d usually start with a background insulin, and because your level is quite high we may add a mealtime dose too. Our diabetes nurse will show you exactly how, and you’d keep your metformin. We’d look at your other tablets as well — some can cause lows once insulin starts.
SCA_MODELS.why: NG28-consistent regimen, practical reassurance and review of hypoglycaemic agents

SCA_MODELS.text: And the driving? That’s my living.

This matters, so I’ll be clear. On insulin, you must tell the DVLA, and because taxi licensing usually uses the stricter rules for professional drivers, you should also speak to the council before you start. They’ll want you to have good awareness of lows, no severe lows, and regular glucose readings. I can’t promise there won’t be any pause in work while they check, but people do carry on driving taxis on insulin — and knowing the rules is what protects your licence.
SCA_MODELS.why: Gives accurate DVLA and licensing-authority advice honestly

SCA_MODELS.text: Right. I’d rather know now than get caught out.

Then the daily rule: check your sugar within two hours before you drive and every two hours on shift. If it’s 5 or under, eat something before you set off. Under 4, or you feel a low coming, don’t drive — treat it and wait 45 minutes after it’s back to normal. Keep glucose tablets in the cab.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific DVLA glucose rules for a working driver

SCA_MODELS.text: And for a low anywhere: sweaty, shaky, hungry, muddled. Take fast sugar — glucose tablets or a small sugary drink — check again after 10 to 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then a sandwich or biscuits. Missed meals and alcohol are the big triggers. How does that sound?
More manageable than I thought.

So where are you now? You don’t have to decide this minute. We could book you with the diabetes nurse for an injection demonstration, you contact the council, and we decide together once you’ve seen it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Shared decision without coercion or capitulation

SCA_MODELS.text: Let’s do the nurse. If I can see it, I think I can do it.

Good. I’ll also make sure your eye screening is up to date, and I’ll note today that I’ve told you about the DVLA and the council. Could you tell me back the two driving rules, so I know I’ve explained them properly?
SCA_MODELS.why: Documents the advice and checks understanding with teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: Test before I drive and every two hours. Under 5, eat first. Under 4, don’t drive, sort it, wait 45 minutes. And tell the DVLA and the council.

Spot on. Once you start, if you have a low that needs someone else’s help, stop driving and tell us. If you’re ill and not eating, ring us for sick-day advice rather than stopping insulin. I’ll see you after the nurse appointment. Anything we’ve not covered?
SCA_MODELS.why: Clear safety-net, sick-day advice and follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: No — I feel a lot better. Thanks, doc.
You’ve not failed at anything. You’re taking the step that protects your eyes, your health and your job.

SCA_STEM.name: Sanjay Mehta
pmh: Latest HbA1c 86 mmol/mol despite maximal oral therapy
meds: Oral glucose-lowering medicines at maximal tolerated doses (details as on the repeat record)
Any GLP-1 receptor agonist as on the repeat record
SCA_STEM.recent: HbA1c 86 mmol/mol on maximal oral therapy. Previous review recommended starting insulin. Works as a taxi driver. Family history: mother had diabetes and lost her sight.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation to discuss starting insulin.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG28 (type 2 diabetes in adults: management, updated February 2026) · [2] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: a guide for medical professionals (November 2025 edition) · [3] DVLA INF294, A guide to insulin-treated diabetes and driving · [4] JBDS-IP, Hospital management of hypoglycaemia in adults with diabetes · [5] BNF insulin monographs
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Needing insulin reflects progressive loss of beta-cell function, not failure. Starting it safely means a structured programme: technique, self-monitoring, titration, hypoglycaemia and the DVLA rules. For a taxi driver the licensing conversation is part of the prescription, not an afterthought.

points.t: NICE NG28 [1] (insulin recommendations amended 2026 for product withdrawals and shortages): offer NPH insulin once or twice daily according to need, or a basal insulin intended for once- or twice-daily use, as initial insulin therapy. Consider basal plus short- or rapid-acting insulin from the start, especially if HbA1c is 75 mmol/mol or higher — his is 86. Continue metformin unless contraindicated and review the other agents, particularly a sulfonylurea (hypoglycaemia risk). Doses per BNF [5].

NICE NG28 [1]: anyone starting insulin gets a structured programme covering injection technique (rotating sites, avoiding repeated injections at one point), self-monitoring, dose titration to target, dietary advice, the DVLA guidance [2], managing hypoglycaemia, managing acute changes in glucose, and support from a professional trained in insulin therapy.

Type 2 diabetes is progressive: beta-cell insulin output falls over time, so most people eventually need treatment intensification. Validate the feeling, then correct the belief. Needing insulin says nothing about his effort.

Retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy follow years of hyperglycaemia. Insulin did not blind his mother; better control lowers his risk. Check his retinal screening is up to date before glucose is brought down.

Symptoms: sweating, tremor, hunger, palpitations, confusion. Treat with 15–20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck after 10–15 minutes and repeat if still low, then a longer-acting carbohydrate (JBDS-IP [4]). Risks: missed meals, alcohol, unplanned exercise, dose errors, a sulfonylurea alongside.

DVLA [2][3]: notify if insulin treatment will last more than 3 months. Check glucose no more than 2 hours before driving and every 2 hours while driving (CGM is permitted, with finger-prick backup). 5.0 mmol/L or below — eat a snack before driving. Below 4.0 mmol/L or hypo symptoms — do not drive; treat, and wait 45 minutes after glucose is back to normal. Must not drive with impaired awareness, or after two or more severe (assisted) hypos while awake in 12 months.

Council taxi and private hire licensing authorities generally apply the DVLA Group 2 medical standard. Group 2 on insulin [2]: full hypo awareness, no severe hypo in the previous 12 months, glucose monitored at least twice daily including non-driving days (CGM allowed for Group 2 since November 2025, with finger-prick backup), and a specialist assessment. He should contact his licensing authority before he starts, so any gap in work is planned rather than a shock.

Record the hypoglycaemia and DVLA advice, that he was told to notify the DVLA and his licensing authority, and his decision. The duty to notify is his; the GMC expects the doctor to explain it and act if a patient keeps driving against advice.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Opened with how he feels about insulin; let him list his worries before any explanation.
Explored his taxi work, shift length, licence type, adherence, and what his mother’s illness meant to the family.
Picked up the four layered fears (failure, his mother’s blindness, needles, losing his livelihood) and followed each.
Idea: insulin means failure and caused his mother’s blindness. Concern: hypos at the wheel and losing his licence. Expectation: to avoid insulin.
Checked HbA1c trend, adherence, current hypos, hyperglycaemic symptoms, renal function and retinal screening status.
Considered adherence gaps, the effect of a sulfonylurea on hypo risk, and whether treatment options have been exhausted.
Screened for symptomatic hyperglycaemia and current hypoglycaemia; stated severe hypo rules for driving.
Explained progressive type 2 diabetes needing insulin per NICE NG28 in plain language.
NG28-consistent regimen, metformin continued, other agents reviewed; structured programme via DSN; accurate DVLA and taxi licensing advice.
Reviewed sulfonylurea hypo risk, retinal screening before intensification, and sick-day advice.
DSN review booked; DVLA and council advice documented; teach-back; hypo and sick-day safety-net; follow-up after nurse visit.

social.t: Taxi driving is his livelihood; any licensing pause means lost income. Plan the timing of insulin with him and his licensing authority.
His mother’s blindness and death shape his beliefs about insulin. Explore it; don’t dismiss it.

legal.t: Insulin-treated drivers must notify the DVLA if treatment will last more than 3 months; glucose within 2 hours before driving and 2-hourly while driving (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive, November 2025; INF294).

Council taxi and private hire licensing usually applies the Group 2 medical standard: full awareness, no severe hypo in 12 months, regular monitoring and specialist assessment. He must inform his licensing authority.

GMC Confidentiality (2017) and its guidance on reporting concerns to the DVLA: the patient has the legal duty to notify. If he keeps driving when unsafe and won’t stop, the doctor may inform the DVLA after telling him.

professional.t: GMC Decision making and consent (2020): present options, benefits and risks, including what happens if he declines insulin; respect his choice and keep the door open.
Record hypo teaching, DVLA and licensing advice, and his decision.

community.t: Diabetes specialist nurse, structured education programme for insulin, and Diabetes UK information on insulin and driving.

redFlags: Symptomatic hyperglycaemia: thirst, polyuria, weight loss — consider urgency and ketones if unwell
Any current hypoglycaemia, especially while driving
Impaired hypo awareness or a severe (assisted) hypo — driving implications
psychosocial: Taxi work: licence type, shift length, income dependence
His mother’s illness and death and what it taught him about insulin
Practical barriers: injecting on shift, storage, eating patterns
ice: Idea: insulin means he failed, and insulin caused his mother’s blindness
Concern: hypos at the wheel and losing his licence and income
Expectation: to be allowed to try harder with tablets

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 86 mmol/mol despite maximal oral therapy — insulin is indicated per NICE NG28, with a structured programme and DVLA counselling.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your pancreas makes less insulin as the years go on — like a battery that runs down. The tablets can only push it so far. Insulin tops up what your body can’t make any more. That’s the illness moving on, not you failing.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought insulin caused your mum’s blindness. It was the years of high sugar. Starting now is how you avoid her path.”
management.psychosocial: Plan around his shifts: timing with the council, glucose checks in the cab, carbohydrate in the car, a DSN session he can fit around work.
sharedPlan: DSN demonstration and structured insulin programme (NICE NG28)
NG28 regimen: NPH or basal once or twice daily; consider adding short- or rapid-acting insulin with HbA1c ≥75; keep metformin; review sulfonylurea
Notify DVLA; contact licensing authority before starting; retinal screening up to date
safetyNet: Hypo: 15–20 g fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 10–15 minutes, then a longer-acting snack; a severe hypo means stop driving and tell us
Sick-day advice: don’t stop insulin when unwell; ring for advice

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Candidates rarely fail this station on insulin pharmacology. They fail on beliefs left unaddressed, vague or wrong driving advice, and a decision that is either forced or abandoned.

items.fail: “Insulin isn’t a failure” said in the first minute, before hearing why he feels that way.
items.why: Reassurance before exploration reads as dismissal; the examiner marks a missed cue.
items.fix: Ask what makes it feel like failure, then reframe with the progressive nature of the disease.

items.fail: Moving past “my mum went blind” with a brief “sorry to hear that”.
items.why: The misattribution is the main obstacle. Leaving it intact means he leaves still believing insulin blinds people.
items.fix: Ask what happened, then explain that long-term high glucose caused her complications and insulin protects him.

items.fail: “Just tell the DVLA” with no rules, or wrong thresholds.
items.why: Driving advice is central for a taxi driver. Incomplete advice is a patient-safety fail.
items.fix: Give the rules: check within 2 hours before and every 2 hours; 5.0 or below eat; under 4.0 don’t drive, treat, wait 45 minutes. Carry glucose.

items.fail: Treating a council taxi licence like an ordinary car licence.
items.why: Licensing authorities usually apply the Group 2 standard; missing it can cost him his job unexpectedly.
items.fix: Ask what licence he holds and tell him to contact the licensing authority before starting.

items.fail: Starting insulin without hypoglycaemia teaching or a review of the sulfonylurea.
items.why: NICE NG28 requires hypo management in the structured programme; a sulfonylurea plus insulin raises the risk.
items.fix: Teach recognition and treatment, and say you will review the tablets that cause lows.

items.fail: Pressing for a yes today, or accepting “no” and ending with nothing.
items.why: Both fail shared decision-making. The station rewards a supported next step.
items.fix: Offer the DSN demonstration, a decision date and documented advice. Check understanding with teach-back.
